newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Tajik capital jittery in wake of peace accord.
newsitem.headline: Tajik capital jittery in wake of peace accord.

text.p: The Tajik government on Saturday hailed a power sharing accord with the key Islamic opposition group but observers warned the deal, which left other armed factions out in the cold, could lead to chaos.

The accord, signed by embattled President Imomali Rakhmonov and opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri in the Iranian city of Mashad on Friday, gives 13 seats of a new 26-member National Commission for Reconciliation to each side.
Rakhmonov's spokesman said Nuri will return to the capital Dushanbe from exile in Afghanistan to chair the commission about two weeks after further peace talks in Moscow on Wednesday.
But diplomats in the mountainous, former Soviet republic warned that disgruntled regional and clan groups sidelined by the deal could use force to undermine the accord and rekindle civil war.
"The players in Tajikistan are becoming increasingly multiple," said a western diplomat based in Dushanbe. "It's no longer just two sides."
The original peace plan, sponsored by the United Nations, had earmarked 20 percent of seats in the commission for other groups, including the once powerful northern Leninabad faction.
Observers also question both Nuri and Rakhmonov's ability to rein in hardline elements inside their own camps, who are fiercely opposed to a compromise.

Last month, the commander of Rakhmonov's elite armoured brigade stormed a town held by a rival warlord without notifying the president, the nominal chief of Tajikistan's rag-tag armed forces, and refused repeated orders to return to barracks.
Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, seen as a potential coup-maker, said at the time he had no faith in the peace talks.

Western observers estimate Rakhmonov controls only up to 20 percent of the country bordering Afghanistan and China. One armed Islamist opposition group operates with relative impunity only a dozen kilometers (8 miles) from Dushanbe.
"There's a semblance of some kind of political agreement," the diplomat said. "But do either of them have the power to implement it?" he asked.
After another wave of shootings in Dushanbe last week, in which two United States embassy guards were among seven killed by unidentified gunmen, the commission is taking no chances.
A special force of around 80 men will be formed from government and opposition forces to protect commission members.
Nor is the United States embassy, which is evacuating dependents of its staff.

The United Nations and the Red Cross suspended operations during a two-week hostage crisis earlier this month, in which several foreign aid workers were kidnapped by an armed gang disowned by both the government and the Islamists.
Some diplomats are considering moving into their embassy compounds and travelling only in armoured cars.

Even Russia, which fearing radical Islam near its southern border has stationed around 20,000 troops in the republic to carry out peace-keeping and frontier duties, appears reluctant to wade into the Tajik mire.

Frightening off foreigners -- who with the rest of Dushanbe's inhabitants scurry home early to be off the streets before dark when unexplained gunfire rends the night -- bodes ill for Tajikistan's war-weary population of 5.7 million.
A ceasefire agreed in December appears to be holding. But Tajiks remain heavily reliant on foreign aid.
The Red Cross has said an epidemic of typhoid fever which had already killed ten, threatened to infect tens of thousands.

Hospitals in Dushanbe are already full to capacity and the disease is spreading outside the capital. But after the hostage crisis, travelling around in conspicuous foreign vehicles to tackle the epidemic is dangerous.
"If there's one more hostile incident against a westerner, it'll be very difficult to persuade any organisation to stay," said an aid worker, who declined to be identified.
